article.overview: A soil particle analyser is a class of instrument that measures the size, shape and distribution of the grains that make up lunar regolith. Grain size and shape are inputs to engineering and scientific models of regolith behaviour, and they vary between samples from different locations and surface ages. The sources reviewed for this article describe laboratory instruments that have analysed returned Apollo samples [1], a miniature scanning electron microscope under development at NASA Marshall [2], and a proposed X-ray tomography payload for a commercial lunar lander [3]. None of the sources reviewed describes a flown, operating soil particle analyser on the Moon.
article.description: The name describes a class of instruments rather than one standard design. Three measurement approaches appear in the sources reviewed: (1) laser diffraction combined with dynamic image analysis, as used by the Microtrac SYNC laboratory instrument, which reports grain size and shape distributions for a small sample and whose image channel records large numbers of individual grains [1]; (2) scanning electron microscopy, in which a focused electron beam scans the sample surface and a backscatter electron detector builds an image that the sources state can give information on grain size, shape, morphology and chemical composition [2]; and (3) X-ray computed tomography, in which many X-ray attenuation images are taken as the sample rotates and a three-dimensional reconstruction gives grain shapes, void sizes and pore geometry [3][4].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a soil particle analyser is to characterise the physical texture of regolith. Particle size and shape describe how the material is distributed and how it may behave when handled. NASA-linked work on the Apollo collection has used a laboratory particle analyser to compare samples. Its abstract reports that sample 10084 has an average particle size of about 24.5 µm, compared with about 72 µm for the Apollo collection average, and that the mature samples in the study have higher sphericity and smaller average size, which the authors attribute to maturity [1]. The same work reports that only sphericity and aspect ratio differed between the four samples, and that aspect ratio is linked to terrain type rather than maturity [1]. In-situ instruments would extend these measurements to surfaces where samples have not been returned. The mSEM programme describes grain analysis as a way to support in-situ resource utilisation and lunar science, and possibly to reduce the need for sample return [2]. The METRIC proposal presents grain size distributions by phase, derived from tomography, as complementary to bulk mineralogy [3].
article.operating_principle: The reviewed sources describe three operating principles, each suited to a different measurement. Laser diffraction infers particle size from how laser light is scattered by the grains in a suspension or dispersed sample, and dynamic image analysis measures individual grain outlines so that shape parameters can be calculated [1]. In the SYNC study, about 100,000 grains per sample were captured by the image channel [1]. A scanning electron microscope forms an image by scanning a focused electron beam over the sample and collecting the electrons it emits. The mSEM design uses a cold field emission electron gun, a focusing lens, a deflection and scanning system, and a backscatter electron detector. The cold field emission gun is chosen because it does not require heating of the emitter, which the source links to lower power use, as well as a long lifetime, high brightness, a small source size and low beam energy spread [2]. X-ray computed tomography reconstructs internal structure from many projection images. In the METRIC XCT concept, the sample tube rotates through 360° in 0.9° steps while a divergent X-ray beam passes through the regolith, and a CCD camera records attenuation images. The reconstructed volume gives particle and void sizes, three-dimensional particle shape, modal volumes and pore geometry [3]. A 2024 study used two laboratory X-ray tomography instruments, together with scanning electron microscopy for the smallest particles, to characterise lunar regolith particles from Apollo 11 and Apollo 14 [4].
article.scientific_importance:
Grain size and shape are central to understanding regolith as a material. Laboratory analysis of returned samples has shown that these properties differ between samples and can be linked to maturity and terrain type [1]. A 2024 study of Apollo 11 and Apollo 14 regolith and JSC-1A simulant used X-ray computed tomography on about 14,000 lunar regolith particles, together with 128,000 JSC-1A particles, and the authors state that the three-dimensional particle database is available through NIST [4][5]. These datasets give engineers and scientists a reference against which simulants and in-situ measurements can be compared.

In-situ analysis would add measurements from sites where no sample has been returned. The sources reviewed do not confirm a flight-qualified instrument for this purpose, so the scientific importance of such a payload remains a design goal rather than a demonstrated result.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a soil particle analyser. The examples below are a laboratory instrument, a development-stage instrument and a proposed flight payload component. Where a mass, size, power or resolution value is not stated in the reviewed sources, it is recorded here as not publicly specified. Values are not comparable across the three examples because they describe different instrument types, stages of development and measurement goals.

examples.name: Microtrac SYNC (laboratory particle size and shape analyser)
examples.type: Laboratory instrument, used on returned lunar regolith samples; not a flight instrument
examples.measurement_principle: Tri-laser diffraction combined with dynamic image analysis; about 100,000 grains per sample captured by the image channel.
examples.manufacturer: Not stated separately in the reviewed abstract; the instrument is named as Microtrac SYNC.
examples.qualification: Laboratory instrument. Not flight-qualified or flown according to the reviewed source.

examples.name: Miniature scanning electron microscope (mSEM), NASA Marshall Space Flight Center
examples.type: Development-stage instrument for in-situ lunar investigations
examples.measurement_goals: Grain size, shape, morphology and chemical composition of regolith, to support in-situ resource utilisation and lunar science.
examples.power_approach: Cold field emission gun does not require heating of the emitter, which the source links to lower power use.
examples.flight_status: Not stated; the 2011 source describes ongoing development only.
examples.partners: University of Alabama in Huntsville, Advanced Research Systems, and academic and industry partners.

examples.name: METRIC X-ray computed tomography (XCT) unit
examples.type: Proposed surface payload component for a Commercial Lunar Payload Services lander
examples.scan_geometry: Sample tube rotates through 360 degrees in 0.9 degree steps; attenuation images recorded by a CCD.
examples.sample_delivery: Honeybee Robotics PlanetVac system delivers sieved regolith to the instruments.
examples.flight_status: Proposed. No launch date, mission assignment or flight-qualification status is given in the reviewed abstract.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No universal dimensions exist for a soil particle analyser. The sources give dimensions only for components: the METRIC XCT sample tube is 3 mm in diameter and 10 mm long [3]. Overall instrument envelopes for the Microtrac SYNC, the mSEM and the METRIC XCT unit are not publicly specified in the reviewed sources.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is not publicly specified for any of the three examples in the reviewed sources. No value has been inferred. A future analyser's mass would depend on its measurement technique, sample handling chain and power and thermal design.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power is not numerically specified for the Microtrac SYNC, the mSEM or the METRIC XCT unit in the reviewed sources. The mSEM source qualitatively links its cold field emission gun to lower power use than a heated emitter, but gives no figure [2].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The reviewed sources do not give a complete environmental specification for any soil particle analyser. Lunar surface operation would involve vacuum, large surface temperature variation, fine dust and radiation. These are general constraints for lunar surface hardware rather than values taken from the sources. Laboratory analysers used on returned samples operate in controlled laboratory conditions. Sample preparation, including sieving and dispersion, is part of the measurement chain and affects the results [1][3].
article.limitations: The reviewed sources cover only a small number of samples. The Apollo comparison in the SYNC study uses four samples [1], so the results cannot be generalised to all lunar regolith. Laboratory measurements also depend on sample preparation. A laser-diffraction result, a microscope image and a tomography reconstruction each measure a different aspect of grain size and shape, so they cannot be compared directly without care [1][2][3][4]. The mSEM and METRIC XCT are development-stage or proposed, and their performance figures are design goals or abstract-level values rather than flight measurements [2][3].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A surface-deployed soil particle analyser would need Earth integration, launch, lunar transfer, landing delivery, deployment, power and data connections, and thermal and mechanical interfaces, as for any surface payload. The METRIC proposal is the only reviewed concept with a stated delivery route. Laboratory analysers such as the Microtrac SYNC are not deployed on the Moon; transportation applies to returned samples [1].
transportation_process: Integrate the analyser or sample-handling chain into a spacecraft or lander payload compartment on Earth.
Launch it into space using a launch vehicle.
Use a lunar lander to deliver it to the surface.
Deploy the sample-handling system, deliver sieved regolith to the instruments, and connect power, data and thermal interfaces.
Return of any sample for laboratory analysis would follow a separate return-chain process, which is not described in the reviewed sources.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: For METRIC, a Honeybee Robotics PlanetVac system delivers sieved regolith to the instruments [3]. Deployment methods for a future soil particle analyser, including power, communications and thermal interfaces, are not specified in the reviewed sources.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Returned Apollo samples provide the reference material for the SYNC study [1]. The mSEM programme and the METRIC proposal show development toward surface use [2][3].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander compatibility can be assessed from the reviewed sources. The METRIC suite is described as intended for delivery on a CLPS lander, but no flight date, mission assignment or lander interface is given [3]. Compatibility with a named lander is not verified.

article.historical_significance: The use of Apollo samples as a laboratory reference for regolith grain size is a significant part of the record. Reported comparisons include sample 10084 against the Apollo collection average [1]. A 2024 study of Apollo 11 and Apollo 14 regolith and JSC-1A simulant used X-ray tomography to analyse about 14,000 lunar regolith particles [4]. The mSEM concept, documented since 2011, and the METRIC proposal illustrate a shift toward in-situ analysis of regolith grain size and shape [2][3]. None of the reviewed sources describes a flown in-situ soil particle analyser.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- **Flight status.** No flown, operating soil particle analyser on the Moon is confirmed by the reviewed sources. The mSEM [2] and METRIC XCT [3] are development-stage or proposed.
- **Missing numerical specifications.** Mass, dimensions and power for the Microtrac SYNC, the mSEM and the METRIC XCT unit are not publicly specified in the reviewed sources. No values have been inferred.
- **Sample size.** The Apollo comparison uses four samples [1]. The 2024 tomography study covers Apollo 11 and Apollo 14 material and JSC-1A simulant [4].
- **Dataset location.** The NIST record states that the 3D particle database is available through NIST, but gives no dataset-specific repository URL or DOI in the record reviewed [5].
- **Vendor claims.** Vendor newsroom material on laboratory analysis of Chang'e-5 samples was found in search results but was not verified from the primary source, and is not used in this article.
- **Images.** No image assets were verified for this draft. No image URLs have been added.

data_quality_notes: No images were researched or verified for this payload; payload.article.images, overview_images and all section-level image arrays are empty by design rather than omitted.

The reviewed NTRS PDF downloads were binary and could not be read by the fetch tool; the NTRS citation pages (HTML abstracts) were used for the METRIC, mSEM and Apollo particle analyser sources instead.
Mass, dimensions, power and resolution are not publicly specified in the reviewed sources for the Microtrac SYNC, the mSEM and the METRIC XCT unit; these are recorded as null.
The Apollo particle analysis comparison covers four samples only; generalisation to the wider lunar regolith is not supported by the sources.
The NIST record does not give a dataset-specific repository URL; the dataset location is unverified.
Vendor newsroom claims about laboratory analysis of Chang'e-5 samples were seen in search results only and are excluded.
The NTRS record 20210026714 full author list and exact title were not verified beyond the abstract content; the author attribution follows the NTRS file name.
